title: Multicriteria Optimization
text:
Decision makers in many areas, from industry to engineering and the social sector, face an increasing need to consider multiple, conflicting objectives in their decision processes. In many cases these real world decision problems can be formulated as multicriteria mathematical optimization models. The solution of such models requires appropriate techniques to compute so called efficient, or Pareto optimal, or compromise solutions that - unlike traditional mathematical programming methods - take the contradictory nature of the criteria into account. This book provides the necessary mathematical foundation of multicriteria optimization to solve nonlinear, linear and combinatorial problems with multiple criteria. Motivational examples illustrate the use of multicriteria optimization in practice. Numerous illustrations and exercises as well as an extensive bibliography are provided.

title: Chapter 2
text:
2.2 Bounds on the Nondominated Set
The ideal and nadir points serve as lower and upper bounds on nondominated points, giving an indication of the range of values that nondominated points can attain. They are often used in compromise programming or interactive methods, the aim of which is to find a most preferred solution for a decision maker.
We assume that \(X_E\) and \(Y_N\) are nonempty, and want to find real numbers \(\underline{y}_k, \overline{y}_k\), where \(k = 1, \dots, p\), with \(\underline{y}_k \leq y_k \leq \overline{y}_k\) for all \(y \in Y_N\).
An obvious possibility is to choose:
\[
\underline{y}_k := \min_{y \in Y} y_k
\]
\[
\overline{y}_k := \max_{y \in Y} y_k
\]
While the lower bound is tight (there is always an efficient point \(y \in Y_N\) with \(y_k = \underline{y}_k\)), the upper bound \(\overline{y}_k\) computed over all of \(Y\) tends to be far from actual nondominated points. A tighter upper bound, called the nadir point, is defined as the maximum taken over nondominated points only.

Definition 2.22 (Ideal Point and Nadir Point)

The point \(y^I = (y_1^I, \dots, y_p^I)\) given by

\[
y_k^I := \min_{x \in X} f_k(x) = \min_{y \in Y} y_k
\]
is called the ideal point of the multicriteria optimization problem \(\min_{x \in X} \big(f_1(x), \dots, f_p(x)\big)\).

The point \(y^N = (y_1^N, \dots, y_p^N)\) given by

\[
y_k^N := \max_{x \in X_E} f_k(x) = \max_{y \in Y_N} y_k
\]
is called the nadir point of the multicriteria optimization problem.

We have \(y_k^I \leq y_k \leq y_k^N\) for any \(y \in Y_N\). Furthermore, \(y^I\) and \(y^N\) are tight lower and upper bounds on the nondominated set.
The ideal point is found by solving \(p\) single-objective optimization problems, so its computation can be easy. On the other hand, computation of \(y^N\) involves optimization over the efficient set, a very difficult problem. No efficient method to determine \(y^N\) for a general MOP is known.
Due to the difficulty of computing \(y^N\), heuristics are often used. A basic estimation of the nadir point uses pay-off tables.

The only case where \(y^N\) can be determined exactly is for \(p = 2\). Here, the worst value for \(y_2\) is attained when \(y_1\) is minimal, and vice versa; through a two-step optimization process, we can eliminate weakly efficient choices from the pay-off table.

Algorithm: Nadir Point for \(p = 2\)
Input: Feasible set \(X\) and objective \(f\) of an MOP.

Solve the single-objective problems: \[
\min_{x \in X} f_1(x) = y_1^I, \qquad \min_{x \in X} f_2(x) = y_2^I
\] Denote the optimal objective values by \(y_1^I\), \(y_2^I\).
Solve \(\max_{x \in X} f_2(x)\) subject to the additional constraint \(f_1(x) \leq y_1^I\).
Solve \(\max_{x \in X} f_1(x)\) subject to the additional constraint \(f_2(x) \leq y_2^I\).
Denote the optimal objective values found in steps 2 and 3 by \(y_2^N\) and \(y_1^N\), respectively.

Output: \(y^N = (y_1^N, y_2^N)\) is the nadir point; \(y^I = (y_1^I, y_2^I)\) is the ideal point.
The optimal solutions of the constrained problems in the second step are efficient. Unfortunately, this approach cannot be generalized to more than two objectives, because if \(p > 2\) we do not know which objectives to fix in the second step.

title: Chapter 1
text:
The solution of a decision problem consists in choosing a “good” or “best” alternative from a set of alternatives, assuming the existence of certain criteria according to which the quality of the alternatives is measured.
Decision problems with a countable number of alternatives are called discrete; others are called continuous.
Discrete problems have finitely many alternatives that are explicitly known, and the goal is to select the most preferred one. Multicriteria decision aid deals with such problems.

title: Chapter 1
text:
1.1 Optimization with Multiple Criteria

Discrete Problems
Discrete problems are decision problems characterized by a countable number of alternatives. The set of alternatives may be either explicitly known or implicitly described through constraints in the form of mathematical functions.


Continuous Problems
In continuous problems, the set of alternatives allows for infinitely many different choices. The feasible set of alternatives is generally given through mathematical constraints, such as functions optimized over the nonnegative real line.
The nonnegative real line is \(\mathbb{R}_+ = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \geq 0\}\).

title: Chapter 1
text:
1.2 Decision Space and Objective (Criterion) Space
This section introduces the fundamental notions of the decision (or variable) space and the criterion (or objective) space, which contain the alternatives and their images under the objective function mappings, respectively. In other words, the decision space is the space of the variable \(x\), and the criterion space is the space of \(y = f(x)\): the decision space is the one that varies, while the criterion (objective) space is the image obtained from it.
Feasible set: the set \(X\), of which every alternative is an element, is called the feasible set, and the space of which \(X\) is a subset is called the decision space.
The image of \(X\) under \(f = (f_1, f_2)\) is denoted:
\[Y := f(X) := \{ y \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y = f(x) \text{ for some } x \in X \}.\]
The image of \(X\) depends on the number of objective functions under consideration, which determines the dimension of the criterion space in which it lies. \(Y\) is referred to as the image of the feasible set, or the feasible set in criterion space. The space from which the criterion values are taken is called the criterion space.
The aspect of decision making concerned with supporting decision makers in selecting a final solution from a set of mathematically “equally optimal” solutions is often referred to as multicriteria decision aid (MCDA).

Definitions

Definition (Decision Space, Criterion Space, Objective Functions, Nondominated Points, MCDA)

Decision space: the space that contains the feasible set \(X\) of alternatives; also called the variable space.
Criterion space: the space that contains the image \(Y = f(X)\) of the feasible set under the objective functions; also called the objective space.
Objective functions: the functions \(f_1, \dots, f_p\) that map each alternative \(x \in X\) to a vector of criterion values \(f(x) \in \mathbb{R}^p\).
Nondominated points: points \(y \in Y\) for which no other \(y' \in Y\) exists that is at least as good as \(y\) in every component and strictly better in at least one.
Multicriteria decision aid (MCDA): the discipline concerned with supporting decision makers in choosing a final, most preferred solution among a set of mathematically equally optimal (efficient) alternatives.

title: Chapter 1
text:
1.3 Notions of Optimality
We now introduce, informally, the concept of “minimization” in multicriteria optimization problems:
\[\min_{x \in X} \big(f_1(x), \dots, f_p(x)\big)\]
The fundamental importance of efficiency (Pareto optimality) is based on the observation that any \(x\) which is not efficient cannot represent a most preferred alternative for a decision maker, because there exists at least one other feasible solution \(x' \in X\) such that \(f_k(x') \leq f_k(x)\) for all \(k = 1, \dots, p\), with strict inequality holding for at least one \(k\). In that case, \(x'\) should clearly be preferred to \(x\).
All the notions of optimality above are, for now, represented only informally; they will be made precise in the following sections.

title: Chapter 1
text:
1.4 Orders and Cones

Orders and Preorders
In order to define the meaning of “min”, we must specify how objective function vectors \((f_1(x), \dots, f_p(x))\) are to be compared for different alternatives \(x \in X\). The different ways of doing this arise from the fact that, for \(p \geq 2\), there is no canonical order on \(\mathbb{R}^p\) as there is on \(\mathbb{R}\). Therefore, weaker notions of order must be used.
Let \(S\) be any set. A binary relation on \(S\) is a subset \(R\) of \(S \times S\). We introduce some properties of binary relations below.

Definition (Properties of a Binary Relation)
A binary relation \(R\) on \(S\) is called:

reflexive if \((s,s) \in R\) for all \(s \in S\)
irreflexive if \((s,s) \notin R\) for all \(s \in S\)
symmetric if \((s^1,s^2) \in R \implies (s^2,s^1) \in R\) for all \(s^1, s^2 \in S\)
asymmetric if \((s^1,s^2) \in R \implies (s^2,s^1) \notin R\) for all \(s^1, s^2 \in S\)
antisymmetric if \((s^1,s^2) \in R\) and \((s^2,s^1) \in R \implies s^1 = s^2\), for all \(s^1, s^2 \in S\)
transitive if \((s^1,s^2) \in R\) and \((s^2,s^3) \in R \implies (s^1,s^3) \in R\) for all \(s^1, s^2, s^3 \in S\)
negatively transitive if \((s^1,s^2) \notin R\) and \((s^2,s^3) \notin R \implies (s^1,s^3) \notin R\) for all \(s^1, s^2, s^3 \in S\)
connected if \((s^1,s^2) \in R\) or \((s^2,s^1) \in R\) for all \(s^1 \neq s^2\) in \(S\)
strongly connected (or total) if \((s^1,s^2) \in R\) or \((s^2,s^1) \in R\) for all \(s^1, s^2 \in S\)



Definition (Equivalence Relation and Preorder)
A binary relation \(R\) on a set \(S\) is:

an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive
a preorder (quasi-order) if it is reflexive and transitive


If \(R\) is a preorder, the pair \((S,R)\) is called a preordered set. In the context of (pre)orders, a more convenient notation for the relation is often used: \(s^1 \preceq s^2\) as shorthand for \((s^1,s^2) \in R\), and \(s^2 \not\preceq s^1\) for \((s^2,s^1) \notin R\), referring indiscriminately to the relation \(R\) or the relation \(\preceq\). This notation can be read as “preferred to.”
Given any preorder \(\preceq\), two other relations are closely associated with \(\preceq\). We define them as follows: * \(s^1 \prec s^2 \iff s^1 \preceq s^2 \text{ and } s^2 \not\preceq s^1\) * \(s^1 \sim s^2 \iff s^1 \preceq s^2 \text{ and } s^2 \preceq s^1\)
Actually, \(\prec\) and \(\sim\) can be seen as the strict preference and equivalence (or indifference) relation, respectively, associated with the preference defining preorder \(\preceq\).

Proposition 1.6
Let \(\preceq\) be a preorder on \(S\). Then relation \(\prec\) defined above is irreflexive and transitive and relation \(\sim\) defined above is an equivalence relation.

Proof.



Proposition 1.7
An asymmetric binary relation is irreflexive. A transitive, irreflexive binary relation is asymmetric.

Proof.



Proposition 1.8
A binary relation \(\preceq\) on \(S\) is:

a total preorder if it is reflexive, transitive and connected,
a total order if it is an antisymmetric total preorder, (so this means that it has to be antisymmetric and a total preorder)
a strict weak order if it is asymmetric and negatively transitive.


Proof.



Proposition 1.9
If \(\preceq\) is a total preorder on \(S\), then the associated relation \(\prec\) is a strict weak order. If \(\prec\) is a strict weak order on \(S\), then \(\preceq\) defined by:
\[s^1 \preceq s^2 \iff \text{either } s^1 \prec s^2 \text{ or } (s^1 \not\prec s^2 \text{ and } s^2 \not\prec s^1)\]
is a total preorder.

Proof.


Most important classes of relations in multicriteria optimization - partial orders and strict partial orders are introduced now.

Definition 1.10
A binary relation \(\preceq\) is called:

partial order if it is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric,
strict partial order if it is asymmetric and transitive (or, equivalently if it is irreflexive and transitive)


Let \(y^1, y^2 \in \mathbb{R}^p\) and if \(y^1 \neq y^2\) let \(k^* := \min\{k: y^1_k \neq y^2_k\}\).
With the (weak, strict) componentwise orders, we define subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^p\) as follows: * \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p := \{y \in \mathbb{R}^p: y \geqq 0\}\), the nonnegative orthant of \(\mathbb{R}^p\). * \(\mathbb{R}_{\geq}^p := \{y \in \mathbb{R}^p : y \geq 0\} = \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p \setminus \{0\}\). * \(\mathbb{R}_{>}^p := \{y \in \mathbb{R}^p: y > 0\} = \text{int } \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\), the positive orthant of \(\mathbb{R}^p\).
Note that for \(p=1\) we have \(\mathbb{R}_{\geq} = \mathbb{R}_{>}\)

Definition 1.11
A subset \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) is called a cone if \(\alpha d \in C\) for all \(d \in C\) and for all \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\) where \(\alpha > 0\).

In other words the cone represent a formula where the vector is multiplied by a constant which has to be greater than 0.
Let \(S, S_1, S_2 \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\). We denote by:
\[\alpha S := \{\alpha s : s \in S\}\]
especially, \(-S := \{-s : s \in S\}\). The algebraic sum of \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) is:
\[S_1 + S_2 := \{s^1 + s^2 : s^1 \in S_1, s^2 \in S_2\}\]
If \(S_1 = \{s\}\) is a singleton, we also write \(s + S_2\) instead of \(\{s\} + S_2\).
More notation, for \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) or \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\):

Definition 1.12

\(\text{int}(S)\) is the interior of \(S\),
\(\text{ri}(S)\) is the relative interior of \(S\),
\(\text{bd}(S)\) is the boundary of \(S\),
\(\text{cl}(S) = \text{int}(S) \cup \text{bd}(S)\) is the closure of \(S\)
\(\text{conv}(S)\) is the convex hull of \(S\)

Definition 1.13
A cone \(C\) in \(\mathbb{R}^p\) is called:

nontrivial or proper if \(C \neq \emptyset\) and \(C \neq \mathbb{R}^n\),
convex if \(\alpha d^1 + (1-\alpha)d^2 \in C\) for all \(d^1, d^2 \in C\) and for all \(0 < \alpha < 1\),

Due to the definition of a cone, \(C\) is convex if for all \(d^1, d^2 \in C\) we have \(d^1 + d^2 \in C\), too: \(\alpha d^1\) and \((1-\alpha)d^2 \in C\) because \(C\) is a cone. Therefore closedness of a \(C\) under addition is sufficient for convexity. Then, using the algebraic sum, we can say that \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) is a convex cone if \(\alpha C \subseteq C\) for all \(\alpha > 0\) and \(C + C \subseteq C\).
Given an order relation \(R\) on \(\mathbb{R}^p\), we can define a set:
\[C_R := \{y^2 - y^1 : y^1 \mathrel{R} y^2\}\]

text:
1.5 Classification of Multicriteria Optimization Problems
By the choice of an order \(\preceq\) on \(\mathbb{R}^p\), we can finally define the meaning of “min” in the problem formulation:
\[
\text{"min"}_{x \in X} f(x) = \text{"min"}_{x \in X} \big(f_1(x), \dots, f_p(x)\big)
\]
The different interpretations of “min,” pertaining to different orders, are the foundations of a classification of multicriteria optimization problems.
With the multiple objective functions, we can evaluate objective value vectors \((f_1(x), \dots, f_p(x))\). However, we have seen that these vectors \(y = f(x)\), \(x \in X\), are not always compared in the objective space \(\mathbb{R}^p\) directly.
The objective function vectors are mapped from \(\mathbb{R}^p\) to an ordered space, where comparisons are made using the order relation \(\preceq\). This mapping is called the model map.
In other words, when we map the objective function vectors from \(\mathbb{R}^p\) to an ordered space, comparisons are made through an order relation \(\preceq\), and the setup is composed of:

the feasible set \(X\)
the objective function vector \(f = (f_1, \dots, f_p): X \to \mathbb{R}^p\)
the objective space \(\mathbb{R}^p\)
the ordered set \((\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\)
the model map \(\delta\)

Feasible set, objective vector \(f\), and objective space are the data of the MOP. The model map provides the link between objective space and ordered set, in which the meaning of minimization is defined.
With these elements we can now define and describe a multicriteria optimization problem:
\[
\big(X, f, \mathbb{R}^p, \delta, (\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\big)
\]
Definition 1.23. A feasible solution \(x^* \in X\) is called an optimal solution of a multicriteria optimization problem \(\big(X, f, \mathbb{R}^p, \delta, (\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\big)\) if there is no \(x \in X\), \(x \neq x^*\), such that:
\[
\delta(f(x)) \preceq \delta(f(x^*))
\]
For an optimal solution \(x^*\), \(\delta(f(x^*))\) is called an optimal value of the MOP. The set of optimal solutions is denoted \(\text{Opt}\big(X, f, \mathbb{R}^p, \delta, (\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\big)\). The set of optimal values is denoted \(\text{Val}\big(X, f, \mathbb{R}^p, \delta, (\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\big)\).
Definition 1.26. A multicriteria optimization class (MO class) is the set of all MOPs with the same model map and ordered set, and is denoted by:
\[
\big[\delta, (\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\big]
\]
For instance, \(\big[\delta, (\mathbb{R}^p, \preceq)\big]\) will denote the class of all MOPs where optimality is understood in the sense of efficiency.

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
To further analyze the subject of Smart Predict+Optimize in the context of inventory management, we need to look at a replicable use case for our problem. Exploring the IEEE competition on Predict+Optimize will give us the correct context.
Optimization problems that must be solved over an unknown future are at the core of many complex real-world operations — supply chaining, inventory management, and staffing rosters, among others. In other words, this applies to everything that involves predicting uncertainty while pursuing multiple objectives. In particular, for this use case, it is important to optimize the solution in light of the global transition to reduce CO₂ emissions.
Renewable energy production is characterized by variability over time, which means it correlates closely with time-series optimization. Demand needs to be predicted and scheduled to make the best use of available supply, with energy storage systems (such as batteries) scheduled optimally to cover shortfalls — all based on unknown future production and demand.
One way to address this uncertainty is through robust optimization or stochastic optimization, using probabilistic forecasts as inputs instead of point forecasts.
Forecasting is often a precursor to optimization, which typically pursues objectives such as minimizing costs, maximizing renewable energy use, or ensuring energy system stability.
Having accurate forecasting is crucial, because it provides the necessary inputs for the optimization model. Without it, the optimization process may rely on incorrect or incomplete information.

In particular, for this use case, it is important to optimize the solution in light of the global transition to reduce CO₂ emissions.
Renewable energy production is characterized by variability over time, which means it correlates closely with time-series optimization. Demand needs to be predicted and scheduled to make the best use of available supply, with energy storage systems (such as batteries) scheduled optimally to cover shortfalls — all based on unknown future production and demand.
One way to address this uncertainty is through robust optimization or stochastic optimization, using probabilistic forecasts as inputs instead of point forecasts.
Forecasting is often a precursor to optimization, which typically pursues objectives such as minimizing costs, maximizing renewable energy use, or ensuring energy system stability.
Having accurate forecasting is crucial, because it provides the necessary inputs for the optimization model. Without it, the optimization process may rely on incorrect or incomplete information.

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling

Predict + Optimize
Now that we have some context on the importance of accurate forecasting and its optimization, it is time to introduce a new concept: Predict+Optimize, where forecasting and optimization are not treated as isolated tasks, but their interaction is taken into account.
Using this approach, forecasts are chosen and evaluated based on their contribution to the actual downstream cost of the optimization problem, in preference to arbitrary forecast measures such as:

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
The IEEE-CIS Technical Challenge
All of these concepts inspired the competition we will discuss: the IEEE-CIS Technical Challenge on Predict+Optimize for Renewable Energy Scheduling. The goal of the challenge was to provide a relevant real-world dataset and optimization benchmark problem, along with strong baseline solutions, to establish a state of the art in the area for the research community.
The main problem originates from the Monash Net Zero Initiative, which involves a campus-wide microgrid equipped with rooftop solar photovoltaic installations and battery storage. This system operates across the entire university campus, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. The university’s objectives are to:

Maximize self-consumption of electricity.
Participate in energy demand response programs.
Keep track of electricity price and yearly peak load tariffs to manage costs.


Initial Data

Energy consumption data
Solar production data
Weather data (ERA5)
Weather data (BOM)
Electricity price data

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
Forecasting
During phase 1 of the competition, participants were expected to predict the power demand of the 6 buildings and the power production of the 6 arrays of solar panels over 15-minute intervals for each day. The actual energy demand of each building and the power production of each array of solar panels were then released. In phase 2, participants were expected to provide the 15-minute energy demand and production forecasts for the same buildings and solar panels for the 30 days of November 2022.
For this section, we are going to analyze the 1st place and 7th place forecasting solutions.

1st Place Solution
The best solution implemented an ensemble of LightGBM, a tree-based algorithm, using calendar features and dynamic features (lags, mean, standard deviation), combined with ensembling models that use daily and weekly weather features.
Their choice of training-set size per series, combined with the optimization approach, produced a methodology that is highly generalizable and robust. They explored several cases and searched for their impact — for example, the time series during COVID provided a great deal of data, making the forecasting horizon diverse across multiple scenarios. On the other hand, the correlation between solar power and buildings’ demand power is highly dependent on weather conditions; the hourly weather data provided by the competition organizers was used for this purpose.
Various statistical models — ARIMA, Random Forest (RF), LightGBM, and SVR — were developed and used for the building predictive models. Although RF and SVR were fairly accurate and competitive with LightGBM, LightGBM was ultimately chosen since it is significantly faster and returns reliable forecasts.
The hyperparameters were also optimized, and the most significant features for each model were selected.

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
Optimization
The main problem was to create a timetable for a set of activities over the coming month, across the set of 6 buildings, with the objective of minimizing the total electricity cost.
Each building was specified by a number of large and small rooms available. Solar production attributable to each building varied between scenarios by assigning one of the six solar time series to the building in each instance.
Activities were specified by the number of rooms required, whether those rooms were large or small, the duration of the activity, the energy load of that activity, and whether it was recurrent or one-off. The battery specifications were matched to be close to the actual scale and performance of two batteries currently in the Monash microgrid. Each battery was characterized by its capacity, maximum charge/discharge power, and round-trip efficiency.
The objective function vector consisted of:

The wholesale energy cost of all energy imported.
A peak load demand charge.
The additional profit of scheduled once-off activities.

More generally, the constraints imposed by the problem include:

Room availability
Precedence constraints
Battery constraints
Activity timing
Energy balance

Conceptually, the activity scheduling problem thus defined is an instance of the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP).

What is the RCPSP?
It is a well-known problem in operations research, where the goal is to schedule a set of project activities within given resource constraints and time windows. Because recurring activities with precedence must be scheduled on different days, the problem also exhibits minimum time lags — the shortest allowable time between the start of one activity and the start of another — as well as maximum time lags.
For this section, we are going to analyze the 1st place and 7th place optimization solutions.


1st Place Solution
In the optimization component, the team reviewed multiple scenarios using sample average approximation, which minimizes the average cost across multiple scenarios. This approach appears reproducible and solid, giving it strong points in terms of robustness.
The objective function for minimizing the total energy cost includes the square of the maximum load. They used a linearization technique to linearize the objective function and developed a mixed-integer linear program that captures all the constraints of the problem.

❓ What is a constraint problem?
Answer:

One of the input parameters of the optimization model is the net base load, which is the difference between the total predicted base load of the buildings and the generation of their solar panels, per time slot.
Their optimization proposal does not rely on a single forecast. Decision-making under uncertainty plays a crucial role in managing energy systems and must be addressed properly. Their proposal was to treat the net base loads at each time step as a random variable within the optimization model, using the so-called Sample Average Approximation Method (SAAM) — an optimization approach that minimizes the average cost of a solution across multiple scenarios (predictive outcomes), rather than relying on just one.

Answer:

However, the 1st place solution focuses only on “local” models for forecasting, meaning models that work on each series separately. The choice of algorithm is not clearly motivated, and some manual, unclear steps remain in the forecasting methodology. As with the 7th place solution, a shared disadvantage is that forecasting does not appear to have received as much attention as in other solutions, which may influence the results. The optimization search is somewhat greedy, showing a degradation in the solver’s solution when using “fix and optimize” compared to a more exhaustive approach.

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
How to Evaluate the Forecast?
The metric used in this case was MASE (Mean Absolute Scaled Error), a commonly used error measure for forecast evaluation, defined as follows:
\[
\text{MASE} = \frac{1}{h} \sum_{k=1}^{h} \frac{|Y_k - F_k|}{\dfrac{1}{M-S} \displaystyle\sum_{t=S+1}^{M} |Y_t - Y_{t-S}|}
\]
where \(M\) is the number of instances in the training series, \(S\) is the length of the seasonal cycle of the dataset, \(h\) is the forecast horizon, \(F_k\) are the forecasts, and \(Y_k\) are the actual values. MASE was calculated individually for each time series and averaged for the final error used to rank the submissions.

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
How to Evaluate the Optimization?
For the optimization evaluation, two components must be taken into account:

Feasibility
The schedules were required to assign a time period to every recurring activity while adhering to the following constraints, for every activity \(a_i\):

The starting period must fall within the week containing the first Monday of the month.
Start time \(\geq 9\).
Finish time (start time + activity duration) \(\leq 17\).
Activity precedence must be observed.
Every battery schedule must respect the battery’s capacity.



Objective
For a feasible schedule, the objective value is computed in terms of the cost of the schedule. The main objective is to minimize the scheduling cost using an objective function \(O\).

title: Predict + Optimize in Renewable Energy Scheduling
text:
Conclusions
By establishing a well-defined, reproducible problem with a realistic setting, the challenge organizers hoped to encourage further methodological developments and comparative evaluations in this domain. For a decision-making project, the main goals are therefore that it must be reproducible and based on a realistic setting.
This competition demonstrated that forecasting and optimization cannot be treated as two isolated components; however, the nuanced interplay between probabilistic forecasting and optimization-based decision-making still requires deeper exploration.
The winning team used stochastic optimization to minimize the expected cost across a number of forecast scenarios.
In the end, learning how to correctly implement Predict+Optimize algorithms helps us understand how to make better decisions based on forecasting results. Generally, for predicting time series, the most common models are tree-based algorithms such as Random Forest, LightGBM, or XGBoost. Based on the probabilistic results from these models, stochastic algorithms are then used for the multicriteria optimization and the objective function vectors — helping us learn how to select the most efficient solution from the solution set, based on the different objectives being pursued. Developing multi-objective optimization frameworks to balance cost minimization with other objectives, could provide more holistic and sustainable solutions. ::: {.qa-card} #### ❓ What is stochastic optimization?

title: Chapter 2
text:
2.1 Efficient Solutions and Nondominated Points

Definition 2.1 (Efficient Solutions and Nondominated Points)
A feasible \(\hat{x} \in X\) is called efficient or Pareto optimal if there is no other \(x \in X\) such that \(f(x) \leq f(\hat{x})\). If \(\hat{x}\) is efficient, \(f(\hat{x})\) is called a nondominated point.
If \(x^1, x^2 \in X\) and \(f(x^1) \leq f(x^2)\), we say \(x^1\) dominates \(x^2\) and \(f(x^1)\) dominates \(f(x^2)\).
The set of all efficient solutions \(\hat{x} \in X\) is denoted \(X_E\) and called the efficient set. The set of all nondominated points \(\hat{y} = f(\hat{x}) \in Y\), where \(\hat{x} \in X_E\), is denoted \(Y_N\) and called the nondominated set.


Theorem 2.2 (Equivalent Characterizations of Efficiency)
\(\hat{x} \in X\) is efficient if and only if any of the following equivalent statements hold:

There is no \(x \in X\) such that \(f_k(x) \leq f_k(\hat{x})\) for \(k = 1, \dots, p\) and \(f_i(x) < f_i(\hat{x})\) for some \(i \in \{1, \dots, p\}\).
There is no \(x \in X\) such that \(f(x) - f(\hat{x}) \in \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p \setminus \{0\}\).
\(f(x) - f(\hat{x}) \notin -\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p \setminus \{0\}\) for all \(x \in X\).
\(f(X) \cap \big(f(\hat{x}) - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\big) = \{f(\hat{x})\}\).
There is no \(f(x) \in f(X) \setminus \{f(\hat{x})\}\) with \(f(x) \in f(\hat{x}) - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\).
\(f(x) \leqq f(\hat{x})\) for some \(x \in X\) implies \(f(x) = f(\hat{x})\).


Proof.


Conditions for the existence of efficient solutions and nondominated points must be our first concern in the study of multicriteria optimization.
It is convenient to consider \(Y_N\) first, and then use properties of \(f\) to derive results on \(X_E\). So let \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) be a set. Then \(\hat{y} \in Y\) is nondominated if there is no \(y \in Y\) such that \(y \leq \hat{y}\).

❓ What is the bicriterion problem?
Answer:

So let \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\). Let
\[
Y_N := \{ y \in Y : \text{there is no } y' \in Y \text{ such that } y' \leq y \}.
\]
In particular, \(Y_N \subseteq Y\).

Proposition 2.3
\[
Y_N = (Y + \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p)_N
\]

Proof.



Proposition 2.4
\[
Y_N \subseteq \text{bd}(Y)
\]

Proof.



Corollary 2.5
If \(Y\) is open, or if \(Y + \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\) is open, then \(Y_N = \emptyset\).

Proof.



Proposition 2.6
\[
(Y_1 + Y_2)_N \subseteq (Y_1)_N + (Y_2)_N
\]

Proof.



Proposition 2.7
\[
(\alpha Y)_N = \alpha (Y_N), \quad \text{for } \alpha \in \mathbb{R},\ \alpha > 0
\]

Proof.



Definition 2.8
Let \((S, \preceq)\) be a preordered set, i.e., \(\preceq\) is reflexive and transitive. \((S, \preceq)\) is inductively ordered if every totally ordered subset of \((S, \preceq)\) has a lower bound. A totally ordered subset of \((S, \preceq)\) is also called a chain.


Theorem 2.9 (Zorn’s Lemma)
Let the preordered set \((S, \preceq)\) be inductively ordered. Then \(S\) contains a minimal element, i.e., there is \(\hat{s} \in S\) such that \(s \preceq \hat{s}\) implies \(\hat{s} \preceq s\).

Proof.



Theorem 2.10 (Borwein, 1983)
Let \(Y\) be a nonempty set and suppose there is some \(y^0 \in Y\) such that the section
\[
Y^0 = \{ y \in Y : y \leqq y^0 \} = (y^0 - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p) \cap Y
\]
is compact (we say “\(Y\) contains a compact section”). Then \(Y_N\) is nonempty.

Proof.



Definition 2.11
A set \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) is called \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicompact if every open cover of \(Y\) of the form
\[
\{ (y^i - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p)^c : y^i \in Y,\ i \in I \}
\]
has a finite subcover. This means that whenever \(Y \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} (y^i - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p)^c\), there exist \(m \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(\{i_1, \dots, i_m\} \subseteq I\) such that
\[
Y \subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^{m} (y^{i_k} - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p)^c
\]
Here \((y^i - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p)^c\) denotes the complement \(\mathbb{R}^p \setminus (y^i - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p)\) of \(y^i - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\). Note that these sets are always open.


Theorem 2.12 (Corley, 1980)
If \(Y \neq \emptyset\) is \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicompact, then \(Y_N \neq \emptyset\).

Proof.



Definition 2.13
A set \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) is called \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-compact if, for all \(y \in Y\), the section \((y - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p) \cap Y\) is compact.


Proposition 2.14
If \(Y\) is \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-compact, then \(Y\) is \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicompact.

Proof.



Corollary 2.15 (Hartley, 1978)
If \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) is nonempty and \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-compact, then \(Y_N \neq \emptyset\).

Proof.


We have been focusing on the existence of nondominated points. Now let us consider the existence of efficient solutions, i.e., conditions that guarantee \(X_E \neq \emptyset\), which is an important issue when practical problems are considered.
We can use Theorem 2.12 and properties of \(f\) to get an existence result for \(X_E\). Theorem 2.19 below is a multicriteria analogue to the well-known result that a lower semicontinuous function attains its minimum over a compact set.

Definition 2.16
A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p\) is \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicontinuous if
\[
f^{-1}(y - \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : y - f(x) \in \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p \}
\]
is closed for all \(y \in \mathbb{R}^p\), i.e., the preimage of the translated negative orthant is always closed.


Lemma 2.17
A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p\) is \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicontinuous if and only if the component functions \(f_k: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) are lower semicontinuous for all \(k = 1, \dots, p\).

Proof.



Proposition 2.18
Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p\) be \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicontinuous. Then \(Y = f(X)\) is \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicompact.

Proof.



Theorem 2.19
Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty and compact set, and let \(f\) be \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-semicontinuous. Then \(X_E \neq \emptyset\).

Proof.



Definition 2.20
The nondominated set \(Y_N\) is said to be externally stable if, for each \(y \in Y \setminus Y_N\), there is \(\hat{y} \in Y_N\) such that \(y \in \hat{y} + \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\).


Theorem 2.21
Let \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) be nonempty and \(\mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p\)-compact. Then \(Y_N\) is externally stable, i.e.,
\[
Y \subseteq Y_N + \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p
\]

Proof.

2.3 Weakly and Strictly Efficient Solutions
Nondominated points are defined using the componentwise order on \(\mathbb{R}^p\). When we use the weak and strict componentwise orders instead, we obtain the definitions of weakly and strictly nondominated points, respectively.

Definition 2.24 (Weakly and Strictly Efficient Solutions)
A feasible solution \(\hat{x} \in X\) is called weakly efficient (weakly Pareto optimal) if there is no \(x \in X\) such that \(f(x) < f(\hat{x})\), i.e., \(f_k(x) < f_k(\hat{x})\) for all \(k = 1, \dots, p\). The point \(\hat{y} = f(\hat{x})\) is then called weakly nondominated.
A feasible solution \(\hat{x} \in X\) is called strictly efficient (strictly Pareto optimal) if there is no \(x \in X\), \(x \neq \hat{x}\), such that \(f(x) \leqq f(\hat{x})\).
The weakly (strictly) efficient and nondominated sets are denoted \(X_{wE}\) (\(X_{sE}\)) and \(Y_{wN}\) (\(Y_{sN}\)), respectively.

From the definition it is obvious that
\[
Y_N \subset Y_{wN}
\]
and
\[
Y_{sE} \subset X_E \subset X_{wE}
\]
As in the case of efficiency, weak efficiency has several equivalent definitions. A feasible solution \(\hat{x} \in X\) is weakly efficient if and only if:

There is no \(x \in X\) such that \(f(\hat{x}) - f(x) \in \text{int}\, \mathbb{R}_{\geqq}^p = \mathbb{R}_{>}^p\).
\(\big(f(\hat{x}) - \mathbb{R}_{>}^p\big) \cap f(X) = \emptyset\).







Note



⚠️ There is no such concept as strict nondominance for sets \(Y \subset \mathbb{R}^p\).


By definition, strict efficiency prohibits solutions \(x^1, x^2\) with \(f(x^1) = f(x^2)\), i.e., strict efficiency is the multicriteria analogue of unique optimal solutions in scalar optimization:
\[
\hat{x} \in X_{sE} \iff \hat{x} \in X_E \text{ and } \big|\{x : f(x) = f(\hat{x})\}\big| = 1
\]
It is obvious that all existence results for \(Y_N\) imply existence of \(Y_{wN}\) as well. However, we shall see that \(Y_{wN}\) can be nonempty, even if \(Y_N\) is empty.

Answer:

Answer:



Theorem 2.25
Let \(Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p\) be nonempty and compact. Then \(Y_{wN} \neq \emptyset\).
